planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil; allow room for the eventual trunk and rounded head to develop, and avoid soils that stay wet through winter.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty or rocky, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade. Blue Nolina is a strikingly architectural Mexican native that slowly builds a stout, palm-like trunk clothed in the persistent skirt of old dried leaves, eventually topped with a dense, rounded head of narrow, flexible, powder-blue leaves with finely toothed margins. Established plants send up tall chartreuse flower spikes in summer and shrug off extreme heat, reflected sun, and long dry spells without complaint, though they benefit from sharp drainage in humid Gulf Coast gardens. Use it as a bold specimen or focal point in xeriscape beds, gravel gardens, or large containers where its sculptural silhouette can be appreciated year-round.

common_name: Toothless Desert Spoon (Blue Sotol, Mexican Grass Tree)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil; choose a site with reflected heat and keep away from irrigation that would leave the crown wet in winter.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil with excellent drainage; toothless desert spoon is prized among sotols for its smooth-margined, spineless, stiffly upright green leaves that form a remarkably symmetrical, globe-shaped rosette without the wrist-slashing teeth of most Dasylirion species. It is markedly more heat tolerant than Dasylirion wheeleri and holds its form beautifully as a clean architectural accent near walkways, pools, and entries where a spineless texture is an advantage. After many years a mature plant develops a short trunk and, on rare occasions, sends up a dramatic flower spike well over ten feet tall lined with small cream flowers that draw pollinators. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it resents heavy or poorly drained soils and wet winter conditions far more than cold.

planting.note: Plant container-grown rosettes in spring in gritty, well-drained, alkaline soil; give it light shade beneath high canopy or full sun in open beds, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay.

directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or sandy loam in full sun to light open shade; Buckley's yucca is a compact, clump-forming Texas Hill Country native with narrow, blue-green, curl-edged leaves that stay low and stemless or develop only a short trunk with age. In mid-spring it sends up dense, candle-like spikes of creamy white, bell-shaped flowers well above the foliage, drawing native yucca moths and other pollinators. It tolerates the dappled shade of oak and juniper woodlands as readily as open sun, making it more flexible than most yuccas for planting beneath high canopy in Hill Country and Gulf Coast gardens. Deer resistant and extremely drought tolerant once established, it is an excellent choice for limestone rock gardens, dry borders, and naturalistic native plantings.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes or offsets in spring into well-drained, gritty soil; allow ample space for the eventual trunk and rosette to reach full size, and position away from foot traffic due to the sharp leaf tips.

directions: Plant in full sun to very light shade in well-drained, gritty or rocky soil; Torrey yucca is a large, dramatic Trans-Pecos and Chihuahuan Desert native that develops a stout, usually single trunk topped with a dense rosette of long, rigid, blue-green leaves edged in curling fibers. With age and adequate room it becomes a small tree, eventually flowering nearly every spring with a tall, dense panicle of white to cream bell-shaped blooms held well above the foliage. It is markedly heat and drought tolerant once established, growing fastest with occasional deep summer water but persisting for decades with none. Give it plenty of clearance from paths and seating areas, since the leaf tips are stiff and sharply pointed, and use it as a bold architectural anchor in xeric borders or gravel gardens.
